name: Mike Walach, Ph.D.
bio: Mike Walach, Ph.D., is an Associate Professor at Montana State University in Bozeman, Montana, and the Principal Investigator for the ASCEND project. His work focuses on unmanned aircraft systems (UAS), high-altitude ballooning, electronics and PCB design, and the development of custom hardware and instrumentation for atmospheric research and STEM education.

Mike holds a Ph.D. in education and has an academic background spanning electronics, technology education, and aviation. His combination of technical and educational experience drives his interest in creating hands-on opportunities for students and educators to explore science, engineering, and aviation.
Outside of work, Mike is a private pilot who enjoys paragliding, powered paragliding, spending time outdoors, building things, and just about anything related to aviation.

name: Sean Bailey
bio: Sean Bailey is a professor in the Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering at the University of Kentucky. He earned his Ph.D. in Mechanical Engineering from the University of Ottawa in 2006, studying the interactions between large-scale rotational flows and turbulence and continued his research on high-Reynolds-number turbulence in wall-bounded flows as a postdoctoral fellow and associate research scientist at Princeton University.

Since joining University of Kentucky, Bailey’s research has combined experimental studies of turbulent flows with the development of new measurement methods. His interests include coherent structures in boundary layers, unsteady vortex flows, interactions between coherent structures and homogeneous turbulence, and the scaling of wall-bounded flows at high Reynolds numbers. Bailey received an NSF CAREER award in 2014 which expanded his work into atmospheric research, including the use of autonomous uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) to measure turbulence in the atmospheric boundary layer. This work has included deploying UAVs to investigate atmospheric boundary-layer turbulence, drainage flows, urban turbulence, sea-breeze evolution, wind-turbine wakes, and stratospheric turbulence.

name: Katelyn Barber, Ph.D.
bio: Katelyn Barber, Ph.D., is an Assistant Professor of meteorology at Valparaiso University, in Valparaiso, Indiana and serves as one of the pod-leads for the ASCEND project. Barber teaches numerous classes involving experiential learning for undergraduate students including instrumentation, instrumentation design, field campaign design, and research collaborations. Barber previously participated in the 2023-2024 National Eclipse Ballooning Project as a team-lead for SUNY Oswego in the Northeast ballooning pod.

Katelyn holds a PhD in Atmospheric Sciences, where her research focused on turbulence generated by thunderstorms in the mid-latitudes and tropics for aviation avoidance. She previously worked at the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory focusing on the transition of shallow tropical clouds to deep convection. Current research interests include the impacts of surface-based ozone on plant species and the transport of surface-based ozone into Northwest Indiana. Barber is also a member of the American Meteorological Society Board on Higher Education.

Barber enjoys (most of the time) supporting the NY Yankees, Buffalo Bills, the NY Knicks, and Manchester City FC. She travels often with her husband and spoils her two cats, Goose and Bernie, who are named after former Yankees players.

name: Matthew Bernards
bio: Matthew Bernards is a Professor of Chemical and Biological Engineering at the University of Idaho in Moscow, Idaho. He also serves as the Director of the NASA Idaho Space Grant Consortium and Idaho NASA EPSCoR programs. Bernards serves as one of the pod-leads for the ASCEND project with a background in atmospheric science high altitude ballooning.

Bernards was recruited into high altitude ballooning in 2018 via a National Science Foundation proposal led by the University of Montana and Montana Space Grant Consortium. This has resulted in him guiding successful balloon campaigns in Chile, the U.S., and Iceland covering both the 2023 annular eclipse, the 2020, 2024, and 2026 total solar eclipses, a Fire Sense demonstration campaign in 2024, and a gulf stream monitoring campaign in 2025.
Outside of work, Matthew enjoys spending time with his wife and two kids, and enjoying the outdoors.

name: Beth A. Covitt
bio: Beth A. Covitt, Head of Science Education Research & Evaluation with the University of Montana’s Broader Impacts Group, serves as the evaluator for ASCEND.

Beth has served as PI, Co-PI, or evaluator on numerous projects addressing STEM education, science literacy, STEM and technical career development, environmental education (especially water and climate), and education partnerships with Indigenous communities. In evaluation work, she adopts a collaborative and participatory approach to (1) facilitate shared understanding of the project’s aims and activities; (2) gather formative information along the way to help the project make decisions about ongoing implementation; and (3) gather summative information to support documenting and reporting on project products, outcomes, and impacts.
Beth has an MS in environmental resource policy and behavior and a PhD in environmental education and conservation psychology, both from the University of Michigan.
Family and friends time, nature time, and reading too much news fill Beth’s hours outside of work.

name: Angela Des Jardins, Ph.D.
bio: Dr. Angela Des Jardins serves as a co-investigator for ASCEND and is a past Science Activation PI. She is a Research Associate Professor of Physics at Montana State University and a solar physicist by training. She serves as Director of the Montana Space Grant Consortium and Montana NASA EPSCoR. In these leadership roles, she is responsible for strengthening education and research initiatives in NASA-related fields across Montana. Dr. Des Jardins is deeply committed to empowering the next generation of professionals in science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM). She is the innovator of the highly successful Nationwide Eclipse Ballooning Project, a large-scale endeavor that engages thousands of higher education students in rigorous, mission-oriented scientific pursuits during solar eclipses.

name: Jie Gong
bio: Jie Gong is one of the subject matter experts (SMEs) of the ASCEND project, with her focus on mentoring ASCEND students in conducting radiosonde and ground weather station data quality control, data analysis and scientific paper/presentation writing. She hopes to engage students in experiencing authentic NASA science data analysis at various levels.

Jie holds a PhD degree in atmospheric science from Stony Brook University and a double-major BS in both atmospheric science and economics from Peking University. She joined NASA Goddard first as a co-op scientist in 2012 and transitioned to civil service in 2022. Jie’s research interests span across multitudes, from ice cloud/frozen hydrometeor remote sensing to atmospheric gravity waves, from boundary layer water vapor to lower atmosphere - ionosphere/thermosphere coupling. Her current projects focus on (1) developing better frozen hydrometeor retrieval algorithms for next generation radiometers; (2) expanding machine learning techniques to better solve atmospheric science problems; (3) understanding lower-upper atmosphere coupling using satellite observations, model simulations and ML techniques. Jie is currently leading the ice cloud algorithm development for multiple satellite missions, including NASA’s FALCON, PolSIR and EUMETSAT’s ICI.
In her spare time, Jie loves to spend time with her two kids and husband at the swimming pool, pickleball court, hiking, reading, watching movies and taking vacations around the world.

name: Eric Kelsey
bio: Eric Kelsey serves as a Pod Lead for the Atmospheric Science track of the ASCEND Project. He’s a Research Associate Professor of Meteorology at Plymouth State University in the White Mountain region of New Hampshire. His research endeavours include understanding snowpack variability in complex terrain, developing an operational snowpack drought index for drought/flood risk assessment, mountain-valley cold air pool dynamics, and atmospheric controls on forest ecosystem water and carbon use at Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest. He has taught various courses since 2012 at Plymouth State including Dynamic Meteorology, Climate Dynamics, Introduction to the Weather Community, Climatology, and Exploring Solar Eclipses. Eric served as the Northeast Pod Lead for the Atmospheric Science track of the NASA-funded Nationwide Eclipse Ballooning Project (NEBP) and co-lead of the Plymouth State University NEBP ballooning team.
Eric earned his PhD in Paleoclimatology from the University of New Hampshire and MS and BS degrees in Atmospheric Science from the University at Albany and University of Missouri, respectively.

Eric enjoys spending time with his family and friends and loves to alpine and nordic ski, ice skate, camp, hike, mountain bike, swim, run, kayak, and just about anything else outdoors. He always has hope for the Red Sox and his garden (sometimes they impress).

name: Marissa Saad
bio: Marissa Saad is the Logistics Coordinator for ASCEND, which is a fancy way of saying she helps with a little bit of everything! From supporting the PI, Pod Leads, mentors, and student teams to juggling communications, social media, reporting, and whatever else comes her way, she's one of the people who’s excited to support you behind the scenes. Marissa uses her past ballooning experience to support ASCEND independently and when she's not wearing her ASCEND hat, she works in a separate capacity as a NASA contractor supporting the Office of STEM Engagement's Performance & Evaluation Team.

Marissa holds a PhD in Teaching & Learning and a master's degree in Space Studies, where her research focused on high-altitude ballooning and technical education. She previously worked for the North Dakota NASA Space Grant Consortium and as the Atmospheric Science Track Lead for the Nationwide Eclipse Ballooning Project (NEBP).
Outside of work, Marissa enjoys running marathons, reading good books, and her latest (and favorite!) adventure: keeping up with her baby daughter, a new addition to the family in 2026.

name: Jill Schmidt, Ph.D.
bio: Jill Schmidt, Ph.D., is an Associate Teaching Professor at Missouri S&T in Rolla, Missouri, and one of the pod-leads for the ASCEND project. She teaches a variety of courses in the Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering program at Missouri S&T, including Introduction to Spacecraft Design, Aerodynamics, Aerospace Structures, and Thermofluid Mechanics.

Jill holds a Ph.D. in Materials Science and Engineering, and has been involved with high-altitude ballooning since her time as an undergraduate student. Since joining Missouri S&T, she has served as a faculty mentor for the high-altitude ballooning program. The Missouri S&T team participated in the 2023-2024 eclipse campaigns as part of the Nationwide Eclipse Ballooning Project, as one of the teams on the engineering track. Jill’s expertise is in the area of payload development for large balloons as well as launching, tracking, and recovery methods.
Outside of work, Jill enjoys hiking, running, and playing board games.
